summary: Jesus takes three disciples up a mountain and is transfigured in front of them — his clothes blazing white, Moses and Elijah beside him, a voice from a cloud telling them to listen to him. They come down to find the other nine failing to free a boy from a violent spirit, and the father saying the most honest sentence in the book: I believe, help my unbelief. Jesus predicts his death a second time, they don't understand and are afraid to ask, and then argue about which of them is greatest. He answers with a child, and with a series of severe warnings about causing others to stumble.
whyItMatters: The gap between the mountaintop and the valley is the whole chapter. Three men see glory; the rest can't help a desperate father; and within a day the group is arguing about rank. Mark refuses to let the vision stand alone.

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching
context.audience: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea; Mark keeps 'Rabbi' and explains Gehenna's imagery by quoting Isaiah rather than assuming knowledge
context.setting: A high mountain, traditionally identified as Hermon or Tabor, then back through Galilee to Capernaum
context.literaryForm: Narrative with a vision scene, followed by teaching gathered into a chain of linked sayings

keyVerses.text: This is my beloved Son. Listen to him.
keyVerses.why: The second time the voice speaks in Mark. At the baptism it addressed Jesus; here it addresses the disciples, and adds an instruction.
The most honest line anyone says in this gospel, and the boy is healed anyway.

keyVerses.text: If any man wants to be first, he shall be last of all, and servant of all.
keyVerses.why: The answer to an argument about rank — not a rebuke about ambition but a redefinition of the ladder.

keyVerses.text: For whoever is not against us is on our side.
keyVerses.why: Said to disciples who had just stopped someone for not being part of their group.

questions.question: Verse 1 says some standing there won't die before they see the kingdom come with power. Did that happen?
questions.answer: One of the most debated sentences in the gospels, and readers land in several places. Some connect it directly to the transfiguration six days later, which Mark places immediately after. Some read it as the resurrection and what followed. Some take it as the coming of the Spirit and the spread of the message. Some see it fulfilled in the destruction of the temple in AD 70. And some hold it as a genuine difficulty about the timing of the end. Mark's placement — verse 1 followed straight by verse 2 — suggests he at least wants the transfiguration read as part of the answer.

questions.question: What is the transfiguration, and why Moses and Elijah?
questions.answer: For a moment the disciples see him differently — Mark reaches for laundry to describe it, whiter than anyone on earth could bleach. Moses and Elijah are the two figures who between them represent the law and the prophets, the whole of the Hebrew scriptures, and both had their own mountain encounters with God (Exodus 24, 1 Kings 19). Their presence says this is continuous with everything that came before. The voice then says something they do not: listen to him.

questions.question: Why does Peter suggest building three tents?
questions.answer: Mark tells you outright in verse 6 — he didn't know what to say, because they were terrified. It is a nervous offer to be useful. The suggestion also has a flaw the story quietly exposes: three shelters would put Jesus on a level with Moses and Elijah, and the next thing that happens is the two of them disappearing and the disciples seeing 'Jesus only.' Mark lets the correction happen in the action rather than in a rebuke.

questions.question: What is the Elijah question about?
questions.answer: Malachi 4:5 promised that Elijah would come before the day of the Lord, and the scribes taught this as a precondition. The disciples have just seen Elijah on the mountain, which raises the timing question. Jesus's answer is that Elijah has already come and was treated however people wished — which the other gospels make explicit as John the Baptist. The sting is in what he attaches to it: the same scriptures that promise Elijah also say the Son of Man must suffer.

questions.question: Is the boy's condition epilepsy?
questions.answer: The symptoms Mark describes — seizures, foaming, rigidity, falling into fire and water — match what we would now recognize as a seizure disorder, and honest readers acknowledge that. The text presents it as a spirit, in the framework its writer and characters used. Christians differ on how to hold that: some take the account as it stands, some read it as an ancient description of a medical condition, some hold that the categories are not necessarily exclusive. What the passage is actually interested in is the father, the failure of the disciples, and what faith looks like when it is exhausted.

questions.question: 'I believe, help my unbelief' — isn't that a contradiction?
questions.answer: It is, and that is why readers have held onto it for two thousand years. The father has just said 'if you can do anything,' which is not confidence, and Jesus catches the 'if.' What the man produces under pressure is not a stronger claim but an honest one: he has some faith and knows it is not enough, and he asks for help with the shortfall. The boy is healed. Mark is showing that what counts is not the quantity of belief but where it is pointed.

questions.question: Why couldn't the disciples do it? They had done this before.
questions.answer: They had — 6:13 says they cast out many demons on their mission. Jesus's answer, that this kind comes out only by prayer, points at the difference. Whatever worked before had started to be treated as a capability they possessed rather than something they had to keep asking for. Note the setting: they are in the middle of a public argument with scribes, with a crowd watching, and a desperate father waiting.

questions.question: Why does Mark keep saying they were afraid to ask him?
questions.answer: Verse 32 is quietly devastating: they did not understand the saying, and they were afraid to ask. It happens right after the second prediction of his death. Mark has already shown them asking plenty of other questions, so the silence here is specific — they have grasped enough to know they do not want the answer. And the very next scene has them arguing about who is greatest, which suggests where the anxiety went.

questions.question: What does setting a child in front of them mean? Children weren't seen as innocent symbols back then.
questions.answer: Correct, and that is the force of it. In that society a child had no legal standing, no status, no ability to advance anyone's position — a person you were responsible for rather than a person who could do anything for you. To an argument about who ranks highest, Jesus responds by putting the least useful person in the room at the centre and saying receiving one of these is receiving him. The image is about status, not innocence.

questions.question: Should I take 'cut off your hand' literally?
questions.answer: Almost no readers across the history of the church have, and the passage itself signals hyperbole — it moves through hand, foot, and eye in a deliberate escalating pattern, and removing an eye would not remove what the eye wanted. The rhetorical form is exaggeration used to force a comparison: whatever it costs to stop is less than the cost of continuing. It is worth reading it as seriously as it is meant, without doing what it does not mean.

questions.question: What is Gehenna?
questions.answer: A real place — the Valley of Hinnom, a ravine outside Jerusalem with a grim history in the Hebrew scriptures as a site of child sacrifice under earlier kings (2 Kings 23:10, Jeremiah 7:31). By this period the name had become an image for final judgment. The quoted line about the worm and the fire comes from the last verse of Isaiah. English Bibles often translate it 'hell,' which imports later imagery; the underlying picture is a cursed valley, permanent burning, and rubbish that is never dealt with.

questions.question: The salt sayings at the end feel disconnected. What holds them together?
questions.answer: They are linked by catchword — fire in verse 49 picks up the fire of the preceding verses, and salt then runs through 49 and 50. This is how sayings were gathered and remembered before books were common, and Mark preserves the chain. The content: salt preserves and seasons, and salt that has lost its distinctiveness has no way to get it back. After a chapter about rank, failure, and severity, the last words are 'be at peace with one another.'

glossary.def: Changed in form or appearance. Mark's phrasing is that he was changed into another form in front of them — the change is in what they can see, not in who he is.
A respectful address for a teacher, literally something like 'my great one.' Mark keeps the Aramaic term.
The prophet taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2). Malachi promised he would return before the day of the Lord, which is what the disciples' question in verse 11 is about.
The Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, associated with child sacrifice under earlier kings and later used as an image of final judgment. Often translated 'hell.'
A heavy grinding stone, the large kind turned by a donkey. The image in verse 42 is of a weight that guarantees no one surfaces.
